usage.description: AlertDialog confirms destructive/irreversible action (delete, revoke access, discard changes). Implements WAI-ARIA APG Alert Dialog pattern (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/alertdialog/): role="alertdialog", aria-labelledby title, aria-describedby description, focus into dialog on open + back to trigger on close, no outside-click dismissal, Escape cancels. Dialog preserves requested width + clamps it to container/dynamic viewport gutters. Generic Dialog footers wrap while consumers own action order. AlertDialog owns confirmation action layout: >640px horizontal buttons may move to another row; <=640px puts the destructive action above Cancel and makes both buttons full width regardless of pointer/hover capability. Button labels remain single-line. Body scrolls when height constrained. Touch (finger or pen): both actions tracked as one group like iOS alerts (action under finger highlights at once, highlight follows finger between actions, lift runs action under finger, lift off both runs nothing); mouse/keyboard/AT keep each button click. Under a finger (phone or tablet), motion like iOS alerts: scales down into place + fades in with the dim on the theme entrance timing, fades out with the dim on the theme exit timing; touch ignored while it appears (keys/AT still act), no input (touch, click, key, AT) while it leaves, a toast it raised stays live; reduced motion = cross-fade only; with a mouse, theme entrance + closes at once. Phone default width 320 (caller width wins). To show w/o managing open state, use useImperativeAlertDialog hook: call alert.show(options) + render alert.element in tree.

usage.description:
AlertDialog asks the user to confirm a destructive or irreversible action before it happens. Use it for things like deleting content, revoking access, or discarding unsaved changes.

It implements the WAI-ARIA APG [Alert Dialog pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/alertdialog/): `role="alertdialog"`, a title linked by `aria-labelledby`, a consequence description linked by `aria-describedby`, focus moved into the dialog on open and returned to the trigger on close, and no dismissal by clicking outside. Escape cancels.

AlertDialog passes its requested width through to Dialog, which clamps the surface to the container and dynamic viewport with token gutters. Generic Dialog footers should wrap, but Dialog does not own action semantics or order; consumer composition controls that. AlertDialog owns its confirmation semantics: above 640px, actions render horizontally and may move onto another row; at 640px and below, the destructive action appears above Cancel and both buttons fill the footer width. Button labels retain their standard single-line behavior. The breakpoint follows available width, not pointer or hover capability. The body scrolls when block space is constrained.

On a touch screen the two actions are tracked as one group under a finger or a pen, the way iOS tracks the actions of an alert: the action under the finger highlights as soon as it is touched, the highlight follows the finger from one action to the other, and lifting the finger runs the action under it. Lifting it off both actions runs nothing. A mouse, the keyboard and assistive technology keep the click of each button.

Under a finger, on a phone or tablet, the alert also appears and leaves the way an iOS alert does: it scales down slightly into place while it and the dimming fade in, on the entrance timing of the theme, and it fades out with the dimming when it closes, on the exit timing of the theme. While it appears a touch does nothing (keys and assistive technology still act). While it leaves nothing reaches it: a touch, a click, a key or an assistive-technology activation does nothing, and a toast it raised stays live. With reduced motion it only cross-fades. With a mouse it keeps the theme entrance and closes at once.

For cases where you want to show an alert without managing open state, use the `useImperativeAlertDialog` hook: call `alert.show(options)` and render `alert.element` in your tree.

bestPractices.description: Express the ratio as a fraction for readability — `ratio={16 / 9}` rather than `ratio={1.78}`. It is a number, so the string form `ratio="16/9"` is a type error.
Use for media that needs consistent proportions across screen sizes.
Use `fit="cover"` for images and video so the component sizes the child; the child should not repeat `width`/`height`/`objectFit` styles.
Pass one child. With `fit` set, every direct child is stretched to fill the box, so put an overlay or caption inside a single wrapper child rather than passing it as a second child.
Describe media children with `alt`, or `alt=""` when the image is decorative. AspectRatio adds no role and no accessible name of its own, so the child carries the whole accessible description.

For a breakpoint-dependent ratio, override the ratio responsively: pass an `aspectRatio` rule via `xstyle` (StyleX), or override `aspect-ratio` from your own unlayered CSS under a `@media`/`@container` rule; component styles live in the `astryx-base` cascade layer, so unlayered consumer CSS wins. Give an `xstyle` rule a `default` branch alongside the conditional one (`{default: 3, '@container ...': '3 / 2'}`); with only the conditional branch the ratio is unset outside the query and the box collapses.
Use for general layout containers; use standard layout components instead.
Nest AspectRatio containers; one level is sufficient.
Constrain the height on its own. The width comes from the container, so a `height` or `maxHeight` by itself clamps the box off ratio; pair it with `width: "auto"` to size from the height instead.
Place it in a shrink-to-fit parent such as `inline-flex`, `width: fit-content` or a floated box. It contributes no intrinsic width there and collapses to zero.

bestPractices.description: Every badge steals attention. Only badge states where the user needs to act. If no follow-up is needed, use plain text.
Use success/warning/error ONLY for system status requiring attention (Failed, Degraded, Action Required). These are visually loud: solid colored backgrounds.
Use color variants (blue, purple, teal) for category tags that classify items: team names, content types, priority levels.
Keep labels to one or two words. If more detail is needed, put it in surrounding text instead of the badge.
Add an icon when it helps identify the badge type quickly, but always include a text label alongside it.

A string or number label keeps its character order under right-to-left, so `+3` and `@alice` read as written. When a rich label mixes directions, mark the direction on your own content, for example with `dir` or `<bdi>`.
Apply "success" badges to every healthy/normal item. If most rows are green "Active", none stand out. Skip the badge for the default state; only highlight exceptions that need attention.
Use badges for metadata. Durations, counts, dates, descriptions → use Text with type="supporting" instead.
Use status variants for non-status info. "6h window", "12 types", category names are NOT statuses.
Repeat loud badges in every row. Common/default states should be plain text; reserve badges for the exceptional.
Make badges clickable; they are read-only. Use a button or link for actions.

bestPractices.description: Every status badge steals attention. Only badge states where the user needs to notice or act: errors, warnings, items requiring follow-up. If no action is needed, plain text is fine.
Use success, warning, and error variants only for system status that demands attention: "Failed", "Degraded", "Action Required". These have bold solid backgrounds designed to stand out.
Use color variants (blue, purple, teal, etc.) for category tags that group or classify items: team names, content types, priority levels.
Keep labels to one or two words. If you need more detail, put it in surrounding text instead of the badge.
Add an icon when it helps identify the badge type quickly, but always include a text label alongside it.

A string or number label keeps its character order under right-to-left, so `+3` and `@alice` read as written. When a rich label mixes directions, mark the direction on your own content, for example with `dir` or `<bdi>`.

Apply a "success" badge to every healthy/active/normal item. If all rows show green "Active" badges, none stand out; the badge adds noise, not information. Show only the states that need user attention (errors, warnings, pending actions).
Use badges for metadata. Durations ("6h window"), counts ("12 trigger types"), dates, and descriptions are not statuses or categories; use description text (Text with type="supporting") instead.
Use semantic status variants (success, warning, error, info) for categories or informational content. These are visually loud and should only indicate system state.

Repeat the same badge in every row of a table or list. If the same value appears in most rows, it's not adding information; use plain text for common states and reserve badges for the exceptional ones.
Make badges clickable; they are read-only indicators. Use a button or link if the user needs to take action.

Open a sheet over another to stack: each sheet keeps its own isOpen, the top sheet is the most recently opened one, the covered sheet recedes and is blocked, one scrim dims the page, and dismissal pops only the top sheet. Sheets rendered in a closing sheet's content leave with it (their isOpen stays yours; they return with the host while still open); siblings above it stay open.

doc.description: A mobile touch sheet that rises from the bottom edge, with animated entrance and exit, a grab handle, optional drag-to-resize snap points, and purpose-controlled dismissal. Like Dialog, it is a padded container: content starts at the theme's bottom-sheet padding (--spacing-4 by default), and a lone Section child or bleed children such as Table and Divider align against it. At the top the content always starts below the grab bar's 24px band, which is not padding a child escapes, so the first row never sits under the bar; scrolled content passes beneath it. A sheet always owns a native <dialog>; inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher the switcher presents and closes that dialog as the flow moves between steps. In both modes, ref and shared DOM props target the visual panel <div>. Sheets stack: a sheet opened while another is open sits on top of it, the covered sheet stays mounted and recedes, and one scrim covers the page. A sheet that closes as another opens in the same update is replaced by it, with the step-to-step handoff a multi-step flow needs.

Automatic calls follow purpose: info dismisses on Escape, scrim click, or swipe; form dismisses on Escape only; required never dismisses implicitly. Omitted only inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher, which drives its steps itself.

Use when the opener can remount or the active element is not a reliable trigger, such as an adaptive presentation switch. Always focused when the sheet closes on its own or last; when a modal sheet is still open beneath, focus returns into that sheet (to this element if it is inside it, else the revealed panel). Omitted only inside the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher, which drives its steps itself.

props.description: Controls implicit dismissal behavior, matching Dialog. info allows Escape, scrim click, and swipe-to-dismiss. form protects entered data by blocking scrim click and swipe while allowing Escape. required blocks every implicit dismissal path and uses role='alertdialog'. Explicit controls may still update the controlled state. Works for standalone and BottomSheetSwitcher-managed sheets.
props.name: purpose

props.description: Deprecated with BottomSheetSwitcher: give each step its own standalone sheet with isOpen instead. Still works as released: the unique ID of this sheet inside a BottomSheetSwitcher, which opens it when activeSheet matches; omit isOpen and onOpenChange when sheetId is used.
props.name: sheetId

props.description: Accessible label for the sheet. Required; the sheet has no built-in heading to derive a name from.
props.name: label

props.description: Sheet content in a scrollable area. The named body is keyboard reachable while overflowing. Forward Tab entry may move directly to the first native link or button; input controls, composite widgets, and nested scroll areas retain the body stop. Shift+Tab from a delegated first child skips the body. Fitting content adds no body stop. The internal observed content box preserves block flow and percentage heights. If it includes a text-entry control that can bring up the mobile keyboard, use height='tall' and keep the sheet fully expanded while editing.
props.name: children

props.description: Internal padding of the sheet content using the spacing scale, matching Dialog. When omitted, uses the theme default for bottom sheets (--spacing-4 unless the theme sets padding on bottom-sheet). A lone Section child escapes the padding, and bleed children such as Table and Divider compensate against it. Use 0 for edge-to-edge content that supplies its own inset. Whatever the padding, the block-start inset is never less than the grab bar's height (--spacing-6), so resting content starts below the bar.
props.name: padding

props.description: How tall the sheet is. Named budgets: 'hug' fits its content up to 92% of the viewport, 'capped' is a scrolling mid-height panel (~62%), and 'tall' is a pinned near-full panel (~92%) for content that streams in. Or pass a number (px) / CSS length for a custom budget. Give snapPoints to let the user drag between heights. On shorter viewports the sheet fills the available height. Only a fully expanded 'tall' sheet provides mobile-keyboard accommodation: it stays put and scrolls each focused control above the keyboard. Hug, Capped, numeric and CSS-length heights never do, and a Tall sheet stops doing it the moment the user drags it to a shorter detent, resuming when they drag it back. Outside that state the sheet neither moves nor adds keyboard scroll space. A TextInput, TextArea or NumberInput in it is scrolled above the keyboard by a scroller in the sheet when that scroller can bring it there; otherwise the page brings it into view, which on iOS can shift the whole page. In Firefox for Android, where the page cannot scroll further, the field can stay under the keyboard. This accommodation applies where the visual viewport shrinks for the keyboard, as in Safari on iOS, Firefox for Android and Chrome on Android, where the sheet places the focused control just above the keyboard as it comes up, and the control rides the rest of Gboard’s slide up, and the slide down after it loses focus; a hide Chrome reports late, such as Back, rides down from Chrome’s report (`astryx docs browser-support`).
props.name: height

props.description: Extra heights the sheet can rest at when dragged; its own height is always the tallest stop, and omitting this gives a sheet that only opens and closes. Each stop is the sheet's visible height: a number is a viewport fraction (0.5 is half the screen), '50%' the same in CSS, '320px' an absolute length. A stop of a quarter of the sheet or less is a peek: it slides away instead of reflowing, and thins the scrim.
props.name: snapPoints

props.description: For a standalone BottomSheet, whether to render a scrim, the semi-transparent overlay that covers and blocks the background. true (default) uses showModal(): top layer, native focus containment, ::backdrop scrim, body scroll lock, and tap-scrim-to-dismiss when purpose='info', with the background inert. A scrim sheet also takes part in stacking (see Stacking below). false presents the sheet in the top layer as a manual popover (below the Popover API support floor, show() in page stacking order as a reduced fallback) with no scrim, no focus trap and no scroll lock, leaving the page behind interactive and scrollable; a no-scrim sheet neither stacks nor is stacked on, but no-scrim steps replace each other with the same handoff. A no-scrim sheet shown while a modal (a scrim sheet or a Dialog) that does not contain it is open is inert under that modal and stays beneath it (show(), no page-level z-index) until that modal has gone, then enters the top layer; a modal mid-exit counts as gone, and rendered inside the modal the sheet enters the top layer at once. In a multi-step flow, set hasScrim the same on every step.

bestPractices.description: Use for mobile-first surfaces (filters, share sheets, quick actions) where the content should rise from the bottom edge.

For a drill-in, open the next sheet over the current one and keep each sheet's isOpen where its data lives; a detail sheet can sit inside the list sheet that opens it, right next to the row. Close every sheet in one update to close the whole flow.
Pick the starting height that fits the content: 'hug' for short bounded content, 'capped' for lists, and 'tall' for forms or streaming/resizing content.
Use purpose='form' to protect entered data from scrim clicks and swipes while keeping Escape available; reserve purpose='required' for flows that must end through an explicit action.
Don't make the sheet content overly long. Break it into steps, each its own sheet, with one state value naming the open step; moving on replaces one with the next.

usage.description:
A mobile touch surface for filters, actions, forms, and detail views that should rise from the bottom of the viewport. For a multi-step flow, give each step its own sheet and one state value that names the open step (see Replacing a sheet); open a second sheet over the first when a step should stay visible beneath it.

Stacking. Every sheet keeps its own isOpen. Open a sheet while another scrim sheet is open and it stacks on top: the sheet beneath stays mounted with its scroll position and inputs, recedes behind the new one (the nearest covered sheet shrinks to 0.96 and lifts 8px, deeper ones to 0.92 and 16px), and is blocked from pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology by the top sheet's modal dialog. The sheets can be siblings, live in separate components, sit inside another sheet's content, or sit inside a BottomSheetSwitcher step; a whole switcher is one level, and switching its step in place does not change its position. Nothing moves in the DOM: each sheet's dialog stays where it is written, and no wrapper component is needed.

Order is open order. The top sheet is the one presented most recently that is still open; a sheet that closes and reopens comes back on top. When several sheets open in one update (a deep link into a flow), there is no open order between them, so tree order decides: a sheet below the sheets rendered in its content, siblings in the order they are written. That order is right in the first painted frame.

One scrim. Only the bottom sheet's backdrop dims the page; the backdrops of the sheets above it are transparent, so a stack never darkens per level. The dim holds steady while sheets push and pop, and if the bottom sheet closes while sheets remain above it, the next sheet's backdrop takes over in the same frame.

Dismissal. Escape, a tap on the scrim, a downward swipe, and a platform close request (Android back, a close watcher) reach only the top sheet, through that sheet's own onOpenChange, and that sheet's purpose applies: required blocks all of them, form blocks the scrim and the swipe. Nothing closes a whole stack at once; set every sheet closed in one update when a flow is done and they leave together.

Closing a covered sheet from code. Sheets rendered inside the closing sheet's content are part of it: they are presented only while it is open and leave with it. Their isOpen stays yours, as with a Dialog rendered in a closed Dialog: nothing is written to it, and a nested sheet that is still open when its host reopens is presented again, on top. Set it closed yourself when the flow is done. Sheets above the closing sheet that are not in its content stay open and keep their order; the closing sheet slides out from beneath them, and if it owned the scrim, the sheet above takes it over.

Replacing a sheet. Close the top sheet and open another in the same update (one state value that names the open step does this) and the new sheet replaces it instead of stacking on it: the new sheet rises above the one it replaces; if the replaced sheet is taller it moves down to meet the new sheet's top edge at the same time; the replaced sheet fades only after both motions finish, and is inert and hidden from assistive technology from the start. The scrim holds steady throughout, with no dip; focus moves into the new sheet; and when the flow closes, focus returns to the element that opened its first sheet, whichever sheet closed last. This is the handoff the deprecated BottomSheetSwitcher ran between its steps; a multi-step flow needs no switcher: give each step its own BottomSheet and one state value. A replace happens only when exactly one sheet closes and one opens in the update, the closing sheet was the top sheet of its stack, and the move was made from inside it (the control last pressed, or with no recent press the focused element, was in the closing sheet, as a step's own Continue or Back button is); a covered sheet closing while a sheet opens, a close and an open in different updates, or a close and an open driven from a control outside the closing sheet (two unrelated owners acting at once) keep the ordinary push and pop motion and their own focus return. A replace over an open stack runs one level up and leaves the sheets beneath covered. Non-modal sheets (hasScrim={false}) replace each other the same way, with no scrim: they are hosted in the browser top layer as manual popovers, so the entering step orders above the retained one with no page-level z-index, and toasts raised before or while the sheet is open stay above it. Below the Popover API support floor (Tier 2 in the browser support guide) the sheet falls back to show() in page stacking order: usable, but with no promise over later page content. A non-modal sheet returns focus to its opener on close only while focus is still inside it; focus taken elsewhere on the live page stays there.

Focus. Opening a sheet, modal or not, focuses its data-autofocus field (a TextInput with hasAutoFocus) in every browser. Without one, focus goes wherever the engine's native dialog focusing steps land: the panel in Chromium, and in Safari on iOS for a modal sheet; the first focusable control in Firefox. So to open on a field in every browser, mark it data-autofocus (a TextInput with hasAutoFocus). A step entering as a replacement also focuses a data-autofocus descendant first, so a flow that opens on a field keeps the keyboard on it. Closing the top sheet returns focus into the sheet it reveals: to the control that opened it when that control is still there, otherwise to the revealed sheet's panel. When the last sheet closes, the standalone rules apply: finalFocusRef, else the element that opened the sheet, with a focus ring only after keyboard input. When every sheet of a stack closes in one update, focus returns once, to the bottom sheet's finalFocusRef or opener, after the last dialog has closed.

Caveats. A Dialog, AlertDialog, or Popover opened from a sheet paints above the sheet and does not make it recede; a sheet opened from inside that Dialog paints above the Dialog and stacks over the sheet beneath. Sheets with hasScrim={false} stay out of the stack entirely (they replace each other, but never stack, recede, or take the scrim). A sheet React hides (a suspended Suspense boundary, Activity mode="hidden") leaves the stack and closes its dialog; when it is shown again it is presented again, on top. Only sheets rendered in the same document stack; a sheet inside an iframe is its own stack.

bestPractices.description: Prefer one standalone BottomSheet per step with one state value naming the open step; the replace handoff is the same and nothing has to be nested under a switcher.

Migrate an existing flow in place: replace activeSheet / onActiveSheetChange with one step value, give each step isOpen={step === id} and a guarded onOpenChange (clear the step only if it is still the open one) in place of sheetId, remove the wrapper and move its hasScrim onto every step. Map the other switcher props: onCancel becomes a guarded onOpenChange on each step (ignore false while the flow must stay open) — a standalone sheet reports Escape, the platform close, the scrim tap and the swipe all as onOpenChange(false) with no reason, so the guard holds the step against all of them while it applies, and a veto of Escape alone has no equivalent; the only per-path lever is purpose (form keeps Escape and blocks the scrim tap and the swipe; required blocks all three and exposes the step as an alertdialog). A consumer aria-label or aria-labelledby becomes each step label, which names its dialog. ref, id, data-testid, className, style, xstyle and the other dialog props have no dialog-level equivalent: a standalone sheet sends its ref and base props to the panel div and its dialog is implementation, so a test or anchor that needs the dialog queries the panel closest("dialog"), and dialog-level styling is dropped.
Don't split information across sheets when people need to compare it; use a full-page layout that keeps the relevant content visible together instead.
Don't use a step flow when multiple panels must stay interactive or visible together; a flow intentionally selects one interactive step.

BottomSheetSwitcher keeps working until a future minor release removes it.

doc.description: Deprecated: write each step as its own BottomSheet with isOpen, controlled by one state value that names the open step. Closing the top sheet and opening the next in the same update, from a control inside the open step, runs the same replace handoff (see BottomSheet, Replacing a sheet), with no sheetId and no switcher; a step changed from a control outside the flow (a page control, or code after focus left the step) closes and opens with ordinary push and pop motion. BottomSheetSwitcher keeps working until a future minor release removes it: a flow used on its own behaves as released (with three fixes: a toast raised from a step renders above the flow and can be pressed, under reduced motion its steps follow the reduced-motion rule, and a step with a hasAutoFocus field opens on that field in every browser), and a flow stacked with other sheets is one level of the stack (it recedes and is blocked when covered, shares the one scrim, and stands down from dismissal while covered). Modal and hasScrim={false} flows migrate the same way. Coordinates multiple BottomSheets as a mutually exclusive flow. One activeSheet ID selects the only interactive sheet; during a handoff, the new sheet enters above the inert previous sheet. If the new sheet is shorter, the previous sheet simultaneously moves down until their top edges align, then fades after both transforms complete. Each child sheet renders its own native <dialog>: a modal flow presents each sheet with showModal(), as a standalone modal sheet does, so the browser supplies modality (the page is inert and focus stays in the top-layer dialog, so both hold across a handoff) and the switcher holds the shared body scroll lock once for the whole modal flow. A no-scrim flow presents each sheet with show() inside the isolated flow wrapper of the switcher, which orders the step dialogs with local values; this differs from a standalone hasScrim={false} sheet, which is hosted in the top layer as a manual popover with no page-level z-index, and it is one reason to migrate. The switcher coordinates the rest: one scrim paints at a time, focus returns to the element that opened the flow, its ref, id, and data-testid resolve to the dialog hosting the active sheet, and its other dialog props and handlers apply to every sheet dialog.

examples.code:
const [step, setStep] = useState(null);

<>
  <Button label="Start" onClick={() => setStep('details')} />
  <BottomSheet isOpen={step === 'details'} onOpenChange={o => !o && setStep(c => (c === 'details' ? null : c))} label="Details" height="hug">
    <SetupDetails />
    <Button label="Continue" onClick={() => setStep('preferences')} />
  </BottomSheet>
  <BottomSheet isOpen={step === 'preferences'} onOpenChange={o => !o && setStep(c => (c === 'preferences' ? null : c))} label="Preferences" height="hug">
    <Preferences />
    <Button label="Back" onClick={() => setStep('details')} />
    <Button label="Continue" onClick={() => setStep('confirm')} />
  </BottomSheet>
  <BottomSheet isOpen={step === 'confirm'} onOpenChange={o => !o && setStep(c => (c === 'confirm' ? null : c))} label="Confirm" height="hug">
    <Confirmation />
    <Button label="Back" onClick={() => setStep('preferences')} />
    <Button label="Done" onClick={() => setStep(null)} />
  </BottomSheet>
</>

usage.description:
Deprecated: write each step as its own BottomSheet with isOpen, controlled by one state value that names the open step. Closing the top sheet and opening the next in the same update, from a control inside the open step, runs the same replace handoff (see BottomSheet, Replacing a sheet), with no sheetId and no switcher; a step changed from a control outside the flow (a page control, or code after focus left the step) closes and opens with ordinary push and pop motion. BottomSheetSwitcher keeps working until a future minor release removes it: a flow used on its own behaves as released (with three fixes: a toast raised from a step renders above the flow and can be pressed, under reduced motion its steps follow the reduced-motion rule, and a step with a hasAutoFocus field opens on that field in every browser), and a flow stacked with other sheets is one level of the stack (it recedes and is blocked when covered, shares the one scrim, and stands down from dismissal while covered). Modal and hasScrim={false} flows migrate the same way. Set activeSheet to a nested BottomSheet's sheetId to open or switch steps, and to null to close.

Stacking. A scrim flow is one level in the stack of open sheets (see BottomSheet, Stacking). Open it while a standalone sheet is open and the flow sits on top of that sheet, which recedes and is blocked; open a standalone sheet while the flow is open, from a step's content or from anywhere else, and that sheet sits on top while the whole flow recedes as one. Switching the step in place never changes the flow's position. Escape, the scrim, a swipe, and a platform close request reach only the top level: the flow's onActiveSheetChange(null) when the flow is on top, the standalone sheet's onOpenChange(false) when that sheet is. A standalone sheet rendered inside a step's content is presented only while that step is the active one: it leaves when the flow switches step or closes, its isOpen stays yours, and it is presented again, on top, if the step returns while it is still open. Only the bottom level's backdrop dims the page. A no-scrim flow stays out of the stack.

dense.description: connected button group w/ shared borders, outer-only radius, horizontal/vertical

bestPractices.description: Group related actions on the same object: copy/cut/paste, undo/redo.
Same variant for all buttons to look like one unit.
Keep groups small (2–4 buttons). Use Toolbar or DropdownMenu for more.
Don't mix unrelated actions in one group.
Don't use for navigation. Use SegmentedControl or TabList.
Don't nest ButtonGroups.
Label the group for what its buttons act on; it is the accessible name.
Single Tab stop; arrows move between members, Home/End to ends (APG roving tabindex).

Under the touch presentation a press tracks like a menu: slide across, the lifted button runs, a lift outside runs nothing. A mouse press acts as a native button's. Finger targets grow toward 44 px, up to half the gap to a neighbour; a menu trigger keeps its own opening.
Don't disable the group for an in-flight action; show progress on the active button instead.

usage.description: ButtonGroup joins related actions into a single connected control. Use for related operations on the same object.

components.description: Groups multiple buttons together with connected styling: shared borders, proper border-radius handling (only on outer edges), and horizontal or vertical orientation. Under the touch presentation a press tracks like a menu: press a button and slide across the others, and the highlight follows. The button you lift on runs, and lifting outside the group runs nothing. A mouse press acts as a native button's. With a finger, each button's target grows toward 44 px, up to half the gap to a neighbour, without the buttons growing. A menu trigger in the group keeps its own opening.

bestPractices.description: Group buttons that perform related actions on the same object, like copy, cut, paste on selected text.
Use the same variant for all buttons in a group so they look like a single connected unit.
Keep groups small (2–4 buttons). For more actions, use a Toolbar or DropdownMenu instead.
Don't mix wildly different actions. A Save button next to a Delete button in the same group is confusing.
Don't use ButtonGroup for navigation. Use SegmentedControl or TabList for switching between views.
Don't nest ButtonGroups. If you need multiple groups, place them side by side with a gap.
Name the group for what its buttons act on. The label is the group's accessible name and a screen reader reads it before each member.

Keep the group a single Tab stop. Arrow keys move between members along the orientation, and Home/End jump to the ends. This is the WAI-ARIA APG roving tabindex technique: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/#kbd_roving_tabindex
Don't disable the group to show that an action is in flight. Leave the group enabled and show progress on the button that started the work.

usage.description: ButtonGroup joins related actions into a single connected control. Use it when multiple buttons represent related choices or operations that belong together visually, like copy/cut/paste, or undo/redo.

Use range mode when user picks start + end dates: trip, time-off request.
Use dateConstraints to disable specific dates (weekends/holidays); explain why unavailable.
Show two months side by side when user frequently selects dates spanning a month boundary.
Custom month view: useCalendarNavigation + useCalendarDays; pass the same calendar to both, feed visibleCalendarMonths into useCalendarDays. Default gregory; never read the provider calendar.
Use for dates far in the past/future; text input is faster.
Disable dates without explaining why.

Use dateConstraints to disable specific dates like weekends or holidays, and explain why they are unavailable.

dense.description: bordered container for DISCRETE items; NOT the default layout tool. Most content doesn't need a card.

propDescriptions.children: content inside card: ONE discrete item; a page’s people/principles/contacts = page content → headings + Dividers or one List, not a Card each (phone too)
propDescriptions.elevation: resting shadow depth: none (flat) | low | med | high (shadow token scale). Raise only to float above content.
propDescriptions.padding: internal padding via spacing scale; omitted = the theme's card padding, NOT a fixed step. Passing a step overrides the theme.
propDescriptions.variant: background color variant; `default` = standard card bg, `transparent` = no background at all, `muted` = muted bg for de-emphasised cards; non-semantic variants use the corresponding `--color-background-<name>` token

bestPractices.description: Ask "could I reorder/remove this independently?" If yes, it's a card. If no, it's just a page section: use heading + Stack or Section.
Use cards for discrete items: one profile, one notification, one metric, one product in a grid. Each card = one "thing" w/ clear interaction boundaries.
Spacing + alignment alone create visual grouping. Not everything needs a container; try removing the card; if grouping still reads from whitespace + typography, skip it.
Keep padding consistent across sibling cards so they align visually in a grid or list.
Pair a card w/ Layout when you need a structured header, scrollable content, and footer with actions.

Card shrinks to its row/grid track, clips unwrappable content at its edge. Long IDs/hashes/URLs → Text maxLines={1} (tooltip shows full value). Wide content → own scroll region (Table scrolls itself; ScrollableArea otherwise).
Default to cards for grouping. Heading + Stack w/ proper spacing creates hierarchy w/o borders everywhere. Cards are the exception, not the default.
Wrap page sections in cards. "General Settings", "Notification Preferences", form groups are page regions; use Section or heading + stack.
Create identical card grids (icon + heading + text, repeated). Vary the layout or question whether cards are needed at all.
Nest cards inside other cards; flatten the hierarchy or use spacing + dividers instead.
Use color variants for status; use Banner or Badge for that instead. Color cards are for categorization.

usage.description: Card is for discrete items with clear interaction boundaries (one profile, one notification, one product). Cards are NOT the default. Spacing and alignment create visual grouping without borders. Ask: "could I reorder or remove this independently?" If no, don't use a card.

bestPractices.description: Ask "could I reorder or remove this independently?" If yes, it's a card. If no, it's just a section of the page: use a heading + Stack or Section.
Use cards for discrete items: a single user profile, a single notification, a single metric, a product in a grid. Each card represents one "thing" with clear interaction boundaries.
Spacing and alignment alone create visual grouping. Not everything needs a container; try removing the card and see if the grouping is still clear from whitespace and typography.
Keep padding consistent across sibling cards so they align visually in a grid or list.
Pair a card with Layout when you need a structured header, scrollable content, and footer with actions.

Let cards share a row or grid on a phone: a card shrinks to fit its track and clips content that cannot wrap at its edge. Truncate long IDs, hashes, and URLs with Text maxLines={1} (the full value shows in a tooltip), and give wide content its own scroll region: Table scrolls by itself; put code or other wide content in a ScrollableArea.
Default to cards for visual grouping. A heading + Stack with proper spacing creates hierarchy without adding borders everywhere. Cards should be the exception, not the default.
Wrap page sections in cards. "General Settings", "Notification Preferences", form groups: these are page regions, use Section or heading + stack.
Create identical card grids (icon + heading + text, repeated). Vary the layout or question whether cards are needed at all.
Nest cards inside other cards; flatten the hierarchy or use spacing and dividers instead.
Use color variants for status; use Banner or Badge for that. Color cards are for categorization.

Most content groups don't need a container at all; spacing and alignment create visual grouping naturally. Only reach for a Card when items need clear interaction boundaries or visual comparison in a grid.

bestPractices.description: Enable scroll-snap when each item should land precisely at the start edge: gallery, product list.
Reach for hasLoop on small cyclable sets (photo gallery) where wrapping past the last item back to the first feels natural.
Always provide an aria-label describing what the carousel contains: "Featured products", "Team members".
Use consistent gap + item width so the carousel looks intentional, not like content overflowing by accident.
Trust built-in navigation: trackpad users swipe horizontally, mouse users hold Shift + wheel to move through items.
Use a carousel for content every user must see. Not everyone scrolls horizontally, so put critical content above the fold.
Auto-advance items. Let the user scroll at their own pace.
Nest carousels. A carousel inside a carousel is confusing and breaks keyboard navigation.

bestPractices.description: Enable scroll-snap when each item should land precisely at the start edge, like a gallery or product list.

For iOS paging under a finger and on a trackpad swipe, pass hasSnap={useSnapPaging()} from @astryxdesign/core/SnapPaging. A flick moves one view, or one item with useSnapPaging({pages: 'item'}). A mouse wheel keeps native snapping. Only a carousel given it loads the paging code.
Reach for hasLoop on small, cyclable sets like a photo gallery, where wrapping past the last item back to the first feels natural.
Always provide an aria-label that describes what the carousel contains, like "Featured products" or "Team members".

Carousel implements the WAI-ARIA APG carousel pattern (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/carousel/) without auto-rotation: the region is labelled and carries aria-roledescription="carousel", each item is a group named "Slide N of M", and the scroll container is a tab stop while its content overflows, so keyboard users can pan it with the arrow keys; while everything fits it stays out of the tab order.
Use a consistent gap and item width so the carousel looks intentional, not like content overflowing by accident.
Trust the built-in navigation: trackpad users can swipe horizontally, and mouse users can hold Shift while scrolling the wheel to move through items.
Use a carousel for content every user must see. Not everyone scrolls horizontally, so put critical content above the fold.
Auto-advance items. Let the user scroll at their own pace.
Nest carousels. A carousel inside a carousel is confusing and breaks keyboard navigation.

bestPractices.description: Compose messages using MessageList > Message > Bubble for consistent sender-aware styling and density.
Set the density prop to control spacing globally: compact for sidebars, balanced for most views, spacious for long-form reading. Individual messages can override.
Use gap when top-level rows are independent (for example, LLM tool events or streamed blocks) and list spacing needs to be tuned separately from density.
Use the group prop on bubbles (first, middle, last) when a single sender sends multiple consecutive messages; it tightens corner radius to visually connect them.
Use ChatSystemMessage with variant="divider" for date separators and default for inline status notices like joins, leaves, or topic changes.
Put name on the first bubble and metadata on the last bubble in a message so they align with the bubble's inline padding.

Wrap custom in-message content (cards, attachments, citations) in a ghost bubble so it aligns with the bubble text column; add width="100%" when it should span the full message column instead of the default bubble width cap.
Provide an emptyState prop so new users see a clear prompt to start a conversation instead of a blank screen.
Use the ghost bubble variant for AI-style responses that show rich content like code blocks or markdown without a visible boundary.
Don't use ChatSystemMessage for sender content; it has no avatar, alignment, or bubble. Use ChatMessage with a sender role instead.
Don't put long or multi-line content in a system message; keep it to a single short sentence. If you need more, use a bubble or a card.
Don't nest ChatMessage inside another ChatMessage; each message is a standalone article element with its own sender context.
Don't apply a fixed height directly on the message list; wrap it in a sized container and let the list fill with flex: 1.
Don't mix filled and ghost bubble variants within the same sender's messages; pick one style per side and use it consistently.
Don't place metadata or names on both the bubble and the message wrapper; pick one based on whether the content has a bubble boundary.

usage.description: Chat is a family of composable primitives for building AI and human chat experiences. Combine ChatLayout, ChatMessageList, ChatMessage, bubbles, system messages, tool calls, tokenized text, and ChatComposer to assemble complete conversations without reimplementing sender-aware layout, density, scrolling, or composer behavior.

doc.description: Layout shell for full chat interfaces. Messages flow in normal page flow, composer is fixed to the bottom with a frosted glass dock. Set density (compact/balanced/spacious) to control spacing, message max-width, and blur layer sizing. Includes built-in auto-scroll, a "New messages" scroll-to-bottom button, and a frosted glass blur layer behind the composer. By default the layout root is the scroll container; pass scrollRef to delegate scrolling to a parent element or the document body. Where the visual viewport shrinks for the software keyboard, the composer stays on top of the keyboard, and a conversation at its newest message stays there. In Chrome on Android the composer rides Gboard’s slides in step with them. In Safari on iOS (in the browser and as a home-screen app) and in Firefox for Android, it moves above the keyboard once the browser reports it. On a touch screen, in a top-level page, every way into the composer’s text (a tap, the keyboard’s previous and next buttons, Tab, the input’s focus()) focuses it without scrolling the page; under a mouse or inside an iframe the browser’s own focus applies. Where your page sets interactive-widget=resizes-content, Chrome on Android shrinks the page for the keyboard itself and the composer stays above it without moving (see the browser-support guide).
doc.name: ChatLayout

bestPractices.description: Keep each value unique within the result list so highlight, active-descendant identity, and selection resolve to the same item.

Inside CommandPalette, each item is an option in the listbox popup of the WAI-ARIA combobox pattern: keyboard focus stays in the query field, arrow keys move the highlight through aria-activedescendant, and Enter selects the highlighted item.

Nest buttons, links, or other interactive controls inside an item. Option semantics make descendants presentational, so use non-interactive content such as icons, descriptions, and shortcut hints, and activate the option itself.
Treat isHighlighted as selection. Highlight is the active keyboard result; isSelected represents the chosen value.

bestPractices.description: Use variant="ghost" with a startIcon for a toolbar trigger. Use alignment="end" when a wide surface should align its end edge to the trigger.
For staged editors, keep draft state in the composed content and call the provided onChange helper only from Apply. Cancel or dismiss without committing.
Compose content from the right accessible structure: RadioList for a simple choice, Calendar/date inputs for dates, TreeList or a searchable list for hierarchy, a custom grid for 2D arrow navigation.
Use the onChange helper from children; it calls both onChange and changeAction and updates optimistic busy state.
Call close() from custom content when a selection should dismiss the popup. Keep it open for multi-step or freeform flows.
Use Astryx focus hooks: useGridFocus for 2D grids, useTreeFocus via TreeList for hierarchies, useListFocus for custom linear collections.
Evaluate custom content against WCAG 2.2: keyboard operation, focus visible/not obscured, names and roles, labels/instructions, target size, and contrast.
Do not rebuild trigger ARIA, popover focus management, or changeAction handling in product code.
Do not use ComplexSelector for a plain single-column text list; use Selector instead.
Wrap a disabled ComplexSelector in Tooltip to explain why it is disabled; the text would not describe the trigger. Use the disabledMessage prop instead.

bestPractices.description: Use variant="secondary" beside secondary buttons, or variant="ghost" beside ghost buttons; add a startIcon when it helps identify the trigger. Use alignment="end" when a wide surface should align its end edge to the trigger.
For staged editors, keep draft state in the composed content and call the provided onChange helper only from Apply. Cancel or dismiss without committing.

Compose the dialog content from the appropriate accessible structure for the job: RadioList for a simple choice, Calendar/date inputs for date picking, TreeList or a searchable list for hierarchy, or a custom grid when two-dimensional arrow navigation is useful.
Use the provided onChange helper from children; it already calls both onChange and changeAction and updates optimistic busy state.
Call close() from custom content when a selection should dismiss the popup. Keep it open for multi-step content or freeform entry flows.
Use Astryx focus hooks for custom content: useGridFocus for two-dimensional grids, useTreeFocus through TreeList for hierarchies, and useListFocus for custom linear collections.

Evaluate custom content against WCAG 2.2: keyboard operation, focus visible/not obscured, names and roles, labels/instructions, target size, and contrast/non-text contrast are especially relevant for selector popovers.
Do not rebuild trigger ARIA, popover focus management, or changeAction handling in product code.
Do not use ComplexSelector for a plain single-column text list; use Selector instead.
Wrap a disabled ComplexSelector in Tooltip to explain why it is disabled; the text would not describe the trigger. Use the disabledMessage prop instead.

bestPractices.description: Keep menu items concise and action-oriented; users expect quick access to contextual actions.
Use sections and dividers to group related actions when the menu has many items.
Use `presentation="adaptive"` when right-click should remain cursor-positioned on desktop while long-press opens a reachable BottomSheet on compact touch devices.
