doc.description: Returns an opaque capability for Table column windowing. Pass the capability to Table.virtualization and keep the complete data, columns, explicit stable idKey and plugins on Table. Columns keep their declared widths: an overflowing Table renders at its minimum width, and the window uses the width each column has there. Pinned columns from useTableStickyColumns always mount; only the columns between the pinned runs window, with a few overscan columns on each side. When the Table's scroll area is at least as wide as the Table's minimum width, every column mounts. A focused cell keeps its column mounted while it scrolls out of view, until focus leaves the Table or moves to another cell. Changing column order, widths, visibility or pinning keeps the first visible column and its scroll offset. Supported tables have one header row, flat rows, no cell that spans columns and single-line content; explicit wrapping, arbitrary custom renderers, non-flat rows, invalid identity, a caller-provided scrollWrapper or a min-width wider than the column floors render every column. To window rows and columns together, pass both capabilities as a list: Table.virtualization={[rows, columns]}. Mounted cells keep native table semantics and full-table column positions; unmounted columns are not promised screen-reader discovery. Keep the capability on the Table for its whole life: adding or removing it remounts the table, which resets focus and scroll position. Changing initialViewportWidth does not remount it.
doc.name: useTableColumnsVirtualization

dense.description: Groups a flat data array into collapsible section rows. Each groupBy value becomes a full-width header (chevron + label + count); collapsing hides its rows, and aria-expanded stays on the button rather than the native row. Returns {data, plugin, idKey}: pass them to Table data / plugins / idKey. Consumer owns the collapsedGroups set. Under pagination the order is filter, sort, slice, group: sort by the group key first so sections stay contiguous and pages append at the bottom. A row-count cut lands mid-section and the heading counts the page, not the section; where the whole result set is in hand, carry the cut to the end of the section it lands in so every rendered section is complete.

doc.description: Hook that groups a flat data array into collapsible section rows. Each distinct groupBy value becomes a full-width section-header row with a chevron toggle, the group label, and a member count; collapsing hides that group's data rows while keeping the header visible. The disclosure state lives on the chevron button, not the native table row. Mirrors useTableTreeState: the consumer owns the collapsedGroups set and the hook returns {data, plugin, idKey}: pass them to Table as data, plugins, and idKey respectively. Grouping runs on the rows you hand it, so with pagination the order is filter, sort, slice, then group: sort by the group key first and the user's keys second, so a section's rows stay contiguous and each page appends to the bottom of the table instead of splicing rows in above the reader. A page that ends on a row count still cuts mid-section, and the heading then counts what has loaded rather than what exists: "6" quietly becoming "10". Where the full result set is in hand, carry the cut forward to the end of the section it lands in: every rendered section is then whole and its count is a total.

T = row type, not inferred from config (defaults to Record<string, unknown>, rejected by typed Table): pass it, e.g. `useTableInfiniteScroll<Walk>(…)`. Three controlled fields: hasMore, isLoading, onLoadMore():Promise<void>. Always-available manual Button; visible sentinel adds automatic loads. Shared latch and post-settlement false commit gate completion. Failure pauses automatic loads; manual retry recovers. Reset by remounting the hook owner and Table together.

A localized Load more Button stays available while hasMore is true; IntersectionObserver adds automatic loading when the end sentinel is visible. The Button remains mounted and focusable while busy and owns the loading announcement.

usage.description: Call useTableInfiniteScroll<T>({hasMore, isLoading, onLoadMore}) and pass the result to <Table plugins={{infiniteScroll: plugin}} />. T is the row type; TypeScript cannot infer it from the config, so it defaults to Record<string, unknown>, which a Table with typed rows rejects: pass it, as in `useTableInfiniteScroll<Walk>(…)` for `<Table<Walk>>`. Keep accumulated rows in your own state. onLoadMore must return a Promise<void> that settles when the batch work completes. A fulfilled request finishes after settlement and a subsequent committed isLoading=false; a true loading phase is not required. Visible short batches can automatically request again in a later task, so update hasMore when the source is exhausted. A resolved request that appends no rows must not incorrectly claim endless more data. Throws, rejections and invalid non-Promise results pause automatic loading; the manual Button can retry once controlled loading is false. The hook does not render product errors or cancel transport. For a new dataset, key and remount the component owning both the hook and its Table, not only the Table child; prevent stale responses from committing caller data yourself. Children mode and unsupported row models do not load and emit a deduplicated development warning. Body modifiers must declare compatible rowModel: flat. Observation uses the Table scroll area while the Table windows its rows, and the browser viewport otherwise, with zero look-ahead and no ancestor discovery. Without IntersectionObserver, the same manual command works.

doc.description: Hook that returns a TablePlugin which prepends a narrow column signaling per-row status. Return {status, label} for a semantic success, warning, or error: Table resolves the matching glyph and tone through the active theme. Return {color, icon?, label} for a custom marker: every color is paint-only, an omitted icon renders the stable 8px dot, and an explicit icon renders that caller-selected glyph. Named custom icons keep their released Icon color mapping; raw CSS custom icons inherit the caller's exact paint instead of the previous primary fallback. Existing callers require no source migration. label is required and becomes the accessible image name plus supplemental hover tooltip; return null for no indicator. The column header is visually blank but carries a screen-reader-only localized name ("Row status", i18n key @astryx.table.rowStatus.columnHeader). Memoize getStatus with useCallback for a stable plugin identity.
doc.name: useTableRowStatus

props.description: Derive either a semantic outcome or a custom marker. {status, label} accepts the closed success/error/warning vocabulary and resolves its glyph and tone through the active theme. {color, icon?, label} preserves the stable custom-marker path: color always selects paint, no icon renders an 8px dot, and icon renders the explicit caller glyph. Even color values named success/error/warning remain dots without icon. Valid icon names: close, chevronDown, chevronLeft, chevronRight, chevronsLeft, chevronsRight, check, success, error, warning, info, calendar, clock, externalLink, menu, moreHorizontal, search, upload, arrowUp, arrowDown, arrowsUpDown, funnel, eyeSlash, viewColumns, copy, checkDouble, wrench, stop, microphone. The branches are exclusive, label is required and announced via role="img", and null leaves the row status cell empty. Memoize with useCallback for a stable plugin identity.

dense.description: Geometry-only fixed-height flat-row opt-in for Table.virtualization. Keep full data and stable idKey on Table. Positive finite CSS-pixel sizes; unsupported content, geometry, identity or a caller scrollWrapper falls back to full rendering. Native mounted-row semantics, not discovery of unmounted rows. Windowed: columns without renderCell, row-number (from 1) and selection columns; any custom renderCell turns windowing off for the table, with a development warning naming the column.

doc.description: Returns an opaque capability for fixed-height flat-row Table windowing. Pass the capability to Table.virtualization and keep the complete data, columns, explicit stable idKey and plugins on Table. Sizes are positive finite CSS pixels. The Table scrolls inside the height its parent gives it and fills all of it. Give the Table's parent a height, fixed or relative, or a flex child, so windowing can bound the rows; with no height every row renders. Make the Table the parent's only child, or a flex child with min-height: 0 beside a heading or toolbar. Supported rows use single-line content; explicit wrapping, non-flat rows or invalid identity use ordinary full rendering. What stays windowed: a column without renderCell (its default cell renders the row's value as single-line text) and the row-number (useTableRowIndex, counting from 1) and selection (useTableSelection) columns. A column with a custom renderCell turns windowing off for the whole table, because Table cannot check that the cell keeps the fixed row height; it renders every row and warns in development, naming the column. A useTableRowStatus column, or a useTableRowIndex column that counts from another number, turns windowing off too. To window a table, put the text a column shows in the row data and leave renderCell off that column. Windowing uses the Table-owned scroll wrapper; a caller-provided scrollWrapper takes diagnostic full-render fallback. Mounted rows retain native table semantics and full-table positions; unmounted rows are not promised screen-reader discovery.
doc.name: useTableRowsVirtualization

props.description: Total body-row pitch in CSS pixels, including existing density padding and collapsed borders. Must fit text and supported controls without reducing their size. props.description: The viewport height in CSS pixels that the first window plans for, on the server and before the viewport is measured. Composable with the other Table plugins: the canonical plugin order places tree before selection, so the checkbox column lands left of the indented tree column. Feed it the treeConfig from useTableTreeState, or construct the config directly for server-driven or pre-flattened trees. When no row is expandable (flat data), every transform is a pass-through and the table renders identically to one without the plugin. Known limitation: the tree column wraps its cell content, so textOverflow="truncate" tooltips do not apply within the tree column.

Use it wherever a truncated cell should show its full content only when it is actually truncated: compose a Tooltip off isTruncated and fullText instead of always rendering one. doc.description: Windowed message list for long transcripts: only the rows near the viewport are rendered, and the rest is represented by two spacer elements, so a thread of thousands of messages costs a viewport of DOM. Rows stay in normal document flow. While a finger scrolls the list, position corrections are written as spacer height rather than a scrollTop jump, so nothing moves under the finger; they settle when that scroll ends. Outside a touch gesture the list writes scrollTop. Follows the newest message by default, re-engaging that follow when a user scroll lands within endThreshold of the bottom. Renders its own scroll container, or nests inside one the caller already owns (see scrollElement).
doc.name: ChatVirtualizer

props.description: Rows to render, oldest first. Changes are detected by REFERENCE, so replace the array instead of mutating it — a mutation leaves the geometry stale.
props.name: data

props.description: Stable identity per row, coerced with String(). The size cache and the running size averages are keyed by it, so deriving a key from the index discards every measurement whenever the list shifts.
props.name: getRowKey

props.description: Renders one row. Row spacing must live inside what this returns (padding) — container gap and margins are invisible to measurement, so the geometry would drift by one gap per row.
props.name: renderItem

props.description: Height assumed for rows that have not been measured yet; a function is authoritative and is never overridden by the running averages. Bias it LOW — an estimate that is too small lets content grow below you and leaves your position valid, while one that is too large shrinks the scroll range and the browser clamps your position into it.
props.name: estimatedItemSize

props.description: Imperative handle exposing scrollToDistanceFromBottomPx and anchorToKey. Both DECLARE a reference frame rather than performing one scroll: the list keeps restoring the declared position as rows measure in, so a landing is not lost to content that arrives after it.
props.name: handleRef

props.description: Classifies a row so measured sizes feed a running average per type. A transcript mixing one-line tool stubs with long markdown then converges to an honest price per shape instead of one blended number.
props.name: getItemType

props.description: Attach mode: the scroll container the caller already owns, into which spacers and rows render as one content block instead of the list creating its own scroller. Pass the ELEMENT, not a ref: a parent's ref attaches after its children's layout effects, so a ref still reads null on the commit that first needs the scroller, and a ref mutation is invisible to React — nothing re-renders and no effect re-runs when it lands, while an element in state makes its arrival a render and a real dependency (scroll listeners, observation, and the gesture state machine are rebuilt when the container changes). Read it in a passive effect and hold it in state. Pass null (not undefined) while it is still pending: undefined means own-container mode, and one commit of that inside an unbounded parent mounts every row.
props.name: scrollElement

props.description: How close to the bottom, in px, a user scroll must land to re-engage following the newest message; disengaging is any upward movement past it. Too tight and a user who stops visually at the bottom (trackpad inertia, fractional row heights, page zoom) silently stops following while output grows below them.
props.name: endThreshold

props.description: Required accessible action name and hover/focus tooltip. Include grouped, unread, or resolved context when it changes the action meaning, for example “Open 4 grouped annotations from Ada and Lin, 2 unread”.

props.description: Non-empty ordered participants, lead first. A single pin renders the first. A grouped pin renders distinct IDs as an AvatarGroup of at most three circles: every participant when three or fewer are distinct, otherwise the first two plus an ellipsis overflow circle. Pass every distinct participant so the overflow appears exactly when more than three people participate. Each record has id, name, and optional avatarSrc.

props.description: Pin height on the element-size scale: sm 28px, md 32px, lg 36px, with 22px, 24px, and 28px participant circles. Padding is equal on every side, so the avatars and overflow sit the same distance from each edge; the trailing count or unread dot adds a little end padding so it never crowds the edge.
props.name: size

props.description: Total represented threads. A finite positive integer above one switches to grouped presentation and displays the exact count. The host still owns the clustering policy.
props.name: threadCount

props.description: Represented threads with unread activity. When above zero, an accent status dot appears at the end of the pin, after the thread total or the single participant; the number itself is not shown. Invalid values are ignored and values above threadCount are capped. Repeat the unread context in label.
props.name: unreadCount

props.description: Whether the pin is the active annotation target. Draws a solid 2px accent outline outside the pin, keeping its elevation, plus aria-pressed; the shared offset focus outline remains farther outside for keyboard focus. Follow aria-pressed toggle semantics: activating the selected pin again should clear the host selection.
props.name: isSelected

props.description: Whether another pin is selected. Lowers this pin’s opacity without disabling it, so it remains available to switch selection. Leave it false on every pin when nothing is selected. Selected presentation wins if both are true.
props.name: isDimmed

props.description: Whether every represented thread is resolved. A resolved pin renders nothing unless it is selected: resolved discussion leaves the content, while a thread the reader opened (or resolved from its popover) keeps its anchor, with the selected treatment, until the host clears the selection.
props.name: isResolved

props.description: Disables activation: the pin exposes aria-disabled, keeps its tab stop, and blocks every activation path. Useful for a pending anchor before its thread exists.
props.name: isDisabled

props.description: Product-owned activation handler. Open or select the represented thread/group here; CommentPin owns no comments or popover state.
props.name: onClick

props.description: StyleX layout customization for the button root. Hosts may position it over content or in a margin; absolute anchors map to the logical bottom-start corner by placing the inline-start edge at the anchor and translating the pin upward by its full height.
props.name: xstyle

accessibility.description: CommentPin is one native button. Tab reaches an enabled pin; Enter and Space activate it. A disabled pin stays in the tab order and is announced as disabled through aria-disabled, and every activation path is blocked.
accessibility.name: Native button activation

accessibility.description: The required label is the button name and tooltip. aria-pressed communicates controlled selection; participant Avatars, the overflow circle, the visible thread total, and the unread dot remain decorative, so repeat grouped and unread context in label.
accessibility.name: Selected state and name

accessibility.description: The solid 2px accent outline hugs the pin while the shared focus-visible outline sits farther outside it, so selection and keyboard focus remain distinguishable; forced colors uses the platform Highlight treatment. Verify both selected and selected-plus-focused states against the host surface.
accessibility.name: Selection and focus

anatomy.description: The compact speech-bubble button surface, with a fixed 2px logical bottom-start corner, 28, 32, or 36px tall by size and padded equally on every side. It owns selected, resolved, disabled, hover, press, focus-visible, and grouped presentation, but no coordinates.
anatomy.name: Marker surface

anatomy.description: One Avatar for a single thread. A group shows its distinct participants as an AvatarGroup capped at three circles: up to three Avatars, or two Avatars plus the overflow indicator when more than three people participate. Avatars are decorative inside the marker; the button label owns accessibility.
anatomy.name: Representative avatars

anatomy.description: An ellipsis AvatarGroupOverflow circle that takes the third position when a group has more than three distinct participants. It shows no number, so the group count stays the pin’s only number. Decorative and non-interactive inside the pin.
anatomy.name: Overflow indicator

anatomy.description: Exact total number of represented threads. Appears when threadCount is greater than one, before the unread dot when there is one; it is a quantity, not ordinal identity. Extra end padding keeps it clear of the pin’s edge.
anatomy.name: Group count

anatomy.description: An accent StatusDot at the end of the pin that marks unread activity whenever unreadCount is above zero: after the group count, or after the participant on a single-thread pin. It adds no second number; decorative inside the pin.
anatomy.name: Unread dot

bestPractices.description: Pass the lead commenter first. For a group, pass every distinct participant ordered by how well they help users recognize the cluster; the pin shows up to three circles and summarizes the rest with an ellipsis.
Write a complete label that names the action and relevant context, such as “Open 4 grouped annotations from Ada and Lin”.
Keep coordinates, zoom/rotation transforms, collision handling, group membership, and thread selection in the host; position the pin with layout composition or xstyle.
Map an absolute anchor coordinate to the pin’s logical bottom-start corner, not its center. Place the pin’s inline-start edge at the anchor and translate it upward by its full height.

When one pin is selected, pass isDimmed to the other pins instead of disabling them. They stay available to switch selection while the active pin holds visual focus. When nothing is selected, no pin dims.
Treat selection as an aria-pressed toggle: when the selected pin is activated again, clear the host selection.
Treat threadCount as quantity only. The Avatar identities stay primary even when the total is large.
Pass unreadCount whenever represented threads have unread activity. Its accent dot keeps unread work visible beside the total; repeat the unread count in label.
Use an ordinal number as the marker identity. Numbering becomes unstable and hard to scan as annotations are inserted, removed, filtered, or grouped.
Put interactive Avatar links or buttons inside the marker. The marker root owns the one action and accessible name.
Slice participants yourself to control the overflow. Pass every distinct participant so the ellipsis appears exactly when more than three people participate, and name the hidden people in label.

usage.description: Use CommentPin as the interactive anchor for comments attached to images, documents, canvases, table regions, or content margins. Pass the distinct participants (lead first), the total number of threads the host grouped at that anchor, and how many of them are unread. The component intentionally has no coordinates, anchor IDs, thread IDs, clustering algorithm, popover, or Comments dependency: those stay with the product so the same marker can sit over transformed media or in normal document layout. Participant Avatars and the overflow circle suppress their own tooltips and interaction; the pin is the only button and its label is the complete action name.

accessibility.description: Each thread has one toggle button (the WAI-ARIA Button pattern, with aria-pressed) named "Thread by" and its author. Enter or Space opens or closes it and keeps focus on it; a pointer press on the thread opens it with focus in the reply composer. The whole surface takes the system focus ring while the toggle has focus.
accessibility.name: Thread toggle

accessibility.description: View replies is a disclosure button with aria-expanded and aria-controls (the WAI-ARIA Disclosure pattern). The more menu follows the Menu Button pattern; when an edit is saved or cancelled, or the delete dialog closes, focus returns to it.

accessibility.description: Focus never drops to the page. After a delete it moves to the next thread, or to the thread when a reply was deleted. Load earlier comments keeps focus on itself, or on the Retry that replaces it when loading fails. A thread selected when the panel mounts opens without taking focus.
accessibility.name: Focus after changes

accessibility.description: Post and reactions stay focusable while a request is in flight and refuse a second press, so focus never drops to the page mid-request.
accessibility.name: Busy actions

accessibility.description: Failures show in error Banners next to the thing that failed, each with Retry when the action can be repeated. A Banner carries no live role of its own: its failure is announced once, assertively, through the shared announcement channel, unless it sits inside the chat log, which delivers it. The progress label of a comment still being written follows the same rule, politely. The edit-history dialog announces its failure through an alert region inside the dialog. A failed delete is announced once, assertively, as the confirmation dialog changes its text.
accessibility.name: Errors

bestPractices.description: Keep the data controlled: update `comments` after each callback. Return a Promise so the panel shows the pending state and, when it rejects, an error with Retry.
Match the surface: give a pane a definite height, use `layout="embedded"` inside a card or popover, and set `container="card"` on a card parent so cards never nest.
For inline comments, keep anchoring in your app: pass each thread its `anchor`, mark it `orphaned` when it no longer resolves, and sync `selectedThreadId` with the passage you highlight.

Keep live state controlled and transport-neutral: map your collaboration layer to `typingUsers` and `seenBy`, and use `onComposerDraftChange` to publish local activity. `seenBy` stays hidden unless a comment render callback presents it. Debounce and expire transient activity in your app.
Put data fetching, authorization, or telemetry in render slots. Keep them in your app and pass the results as data.
Assume `selectedThreadId` moves focus or opens a composer. It reveals and scrolls the controlled thread without interrupting the viewer; only their Reply action opens the reply composer.

usage.description: The Comments panel shows the conversation about a document, task, or record: its comment threads and activity, with a composer for new comments. Use it as a side panel or section that fills a sized container, or embedded at its content height inside a card or popover. Render a single thread with CommentThread and a standalone composer with CommentComposer.

bestPractices.description: In a card or popover: `container="card"`, card padding 0. Thread owns insets, draws no outer rules.
Control `isSelected` when opened from elsewhere (a document highlight). Reveals body and replies without moving focus or opening the composer.

In a Popover over a document: pass `onDismiss`, set `hasLightDismiss={false}` and `hasEscapeDismiss={false}` on the host. Outside press or Escape closes; the first over an unsaved reply/edit shakes and keeps the draft.
Map collaboration state to `typingUsers`/`seenBy`; publish local drafts via `onComposerDraftChange`. `seenBy` hidden unless a render callback shows it. No connections, no participant expiry.
Stack CommentThreads plus a composer as a discussion. Use Comments.
Wrap the thread in your own button/link. It is already one toggle.
Keep host Popover light dismiss on with `onDismiss`. The browser closes it before the thread can keep a draft.

bestPractices.description: Inside a card or popover, set `container="card"` and give the card no padding: the thread supplies its own insets and draws no outer rules.
Control `isSelected` when the thread opens from elsewhere, such as its highlight in a document. Controlled selection reveals the body and replies without moving focus or opening the reply composer.

In a Popover over a document, pass `onDismiss` and pair it with `hasLightDismiss={false}` and `hasEscapeDismiss={false}` on the host Popover. A press outside the thread or Escape then closes it, except that the first one over an unsaved reply or edit shakes the thread and keeps the draft.

Map your collaboration state to `typingUsers` and `seenBy`, then publish local reply and edit activity with `onComposerDraftChange`. `seenBy` stays hidden unless a comment render callback presents it. The thread never opens a connection or expires participants.
Stack several CommentThreads with a composer to build a discussion. Use Comments, which keeps one thread open at a time and orders threads with activity.
Wrap the thread in your own button or link to open it. The thread is already one toggle; a second control nests interactive elements.
Leave the host Popover’s light dismiss on while passing `onDismiss`. The browser closes the Popover before the thread can keep a draft.

While code overflows sideways, sideways overscroll (elastic bounce, swipe navigation) is off.

bestPractices.description: Render one DiffViewer per file and lay out the list yourself; parseUnifiedDiff(patch).map(file => <DiffViewer key={file.newPath ?? file.oldPath} file={file} />) is the multi-file case.
Anchor review comments with the DiffViewerLineRef side + lineNumber pair: it is the same in unified and split view.
Put file-level actions such as a "Viewed" checkbox in headerEnd, and drive isCollapsed from the same state if viewed files should fold away.
Use DiffViewer for a short diff inside prose or a chat message; a CodeBlock with isDiff (or a ```diff fence in Markdown) is the lighter fit there.

usage.description: Read-only, syntax-highlighted diff of one file for code review surfaces. Renders a file header (path, Added/Deleted/Renamed token, +/− line counts, a headerEnd slot, and an optional disclosure) over the file's hunks in unified or split (side-by-side) view. Rows use the same syntax-theme diff slots as CodeBlock with isDiff, so one syntax theme styles both. renderLineAnnotation adds a full-width row under any line (for review comments) and onLineNumberClick turns line numbers into buttons. Build the file model with parseUnifiedDiff(patch), which returns one file per file in a git or diff -u patch, or with createDiffFile({oldValue, newValue}) when you hold two versions of a text. Display options cover how a change is marked (classic +/− glyphs, bars, or none), whether changed rows are tinted, and word- or character-level highlighting of what changed inside each removed/added line pair. Each changed line carries a visually hidden "Added"/"Removed" label, so the change reads without colour in every mode. Unwrapped, line numbers and change indicators stay pinned while the code scrolls; in split view each side is its own scroller, so the split stays fixed at half and half, the sides scroll sideways in lockstep, and a row is as tall as its taller side. While code overflows sideways, sideways overscroll is off, so trackpads neither bounce past a line nor swipe the browser back. In right-to-left pages the hunk area stays left-to-right, like a code editor: annotation content reads in the page direction, and annotation rows scroll with the code. When a change is too large to compare line by line, createDiffFile marks its hunk with isReplacedBlock: it lists every old line as removed and every new line as added. DiffViewer folds those lines behind a "Large change: N lines" row, where N counts the block's removed plus added lines, with a Show full diff button. A file with more than 2,000 other changed lines starts folded the same way, because every row costs render time. Its line diff is still there when the reader opens it. A fold opens by itself when a line it would hide has an annotation, so no review comment is hidden. Rows are plain DOM with no virtualization: collapse or window very large files.

propDescriptions.children: Content to clamp. Composable version of maxLines — wraps arbitrary children.

bestPractices.description: Use for clamping a block of mixed/composed content, not a single Text node.
Use Text's own maxLines for a single Text node instead.
Disable tooltip when content is reachable elsewhere, to avoid redundant announcement.

Inert only for a focusable in the clamp's own flow whose box lies wholly past the last visible line (a positioned element placed against an in-flow containing block in the clamp, like a control's own wrapper, is in the flow and judged by that block's box); never inside a fixed, escaping absolute, top-layer or portaled subtree; a partly visible control stays reachable; a focusable with no box counts as past the last line until it gains a box; re-checked on size, content and font changes. Gap: an absolutely placed control the clamp clips stays a tab stop. Never the focused element, never your own tabIndex or aria-hidden.

usage.description: Wrap any children (mixed inline content, nested elements) to clamp the whole block to N lines. Reuses useTruncation for overflow detection.

props.description: Content to clamp: mixed inline content, nested elements, anything you would rather not wrap in a single Text.
props.name: children

props.description: Maximum number of lines to show before clamping with an ellipsis.
props.name: maxLines

props.description: Show a tooltip with the full text content on hover or keyboard focus when clamped. A clamped root is focusable (tabindex 0) so keyboard users can reach the tooltip; a tabIndex you pass wins. The tooltip props follow Text's: when Text's hasTruncateTooltip is renamed in a minor, LineClamp follows.
props.name: hasTruncateTooltip

props.description: Where the truncation tooltip opens.
props.name: truncateTooltipPlacement

props.description: HTML element to render.
props.name: as

bestPractices.description: Use LineClamp when clamping a block of mixed or composed content (not a single Text node).
Use Text's own maxLines prop when clamping a single Text node — no need to wrap it in LineClamp.
Disable the tooltip (hasTruncateTooltip={false}) when the clamped content is already reachable elsewhere on the page, to avoid a redundant announcement.

LineClamp makes a focusable descendant inert only when both hold: (1) it is in the clamp's own flow. A positioned element is in that flow when its containing block is an element inside the clamp that is itself in the flow, as a control's own positioned wrapper is; the line test then applies to that containing block's box. A fixed element, an absolute element whose containing block is the clamp itself or lies outside it, a top-layer element (a popover or dialog), and anything rendered elsewhere through a portal each start a subtree that is never made inert, at any depth. (2) its box lies wholly beyond the clamp's last visible line. A control any part of which is visible stays reachable. A focusable with no box when LineClamp checks is treated as beyond the last line until it gains a box; LineClamp re-checks then. LineClamp re-checks when its size, its content or its fonts change. Gap: an absolutely placed control that the clamp itself clips stays a tab stop; the author owns positioned content inside a clamp. Inert takes such a control out of the Tab order and the accessibility tree. LineClamp never rewrites your own tabIndex or aria-hidden, and the element that holds focus is never made inert.

usage.description: Clamps arbitrary content to a fixed number of lines with an ellipsis. Text's maxLines clamps a Text element; LineClamp clamps whatever it wraps and adds no typography of its own, so it suits mixed inline content and nested elements without changing their font, color or wrapping. Truncation detection reuses useTruncation (the same hook Text uses), so overflow is measured correctly even while -webkit-line-clamp clips scrollHeight.

props.description: Makes the records reorderable: pass the object createReorderable makes, keyed by getItemKey. Each record ends with core List's reorder handle, after Remove, as UIKit's reorder control ends an editing row. The handle appears while the record is hovered or holds keyboard focus and stays visible on touch screens. On a touch screen, hold the handle for a moment, then drag: the record stays in its place, dimmed, while a copy of it follows the finger and an accent line marks where it would land; the other records stay still, the list autoscrolls near its edges, and on release the records rearrange. A flick on the handle scrolls and a pinch zooms the page. A mouse drags at once the same way, and the records take their places without motion. Activating the handle (a tap, a click, Space or Enter) turns on reorder mode for its record: the line marks the record's place, each Arrow Up or Arrow Down moves it a place, a hint shows the moves and Done as buttons, and Escape or Done ends the mode, keeping the moves. The object's isReorderable(key) says which records move: one it rejects has no handle. Each move goes to the object's onReorder({key, to}), to being the record's index in value after the move. In a disabled or loading list the handles stay focusable but move nothing. Without it, the records keep their order.

anatomy.description: Consumer-rendered inputs that receive scoped record state, complete validation status, the native tooltip status variant, and update behavior. When stacked responsively, label-to-input spacing is smallest, field spacing is larger, and record groups use 32px separation so each object remains visually distinct.

anatomy.description: Removes its record immediately, moves focus to a predictable neighboring control, and animates surviving rows into their new positions when supported. It is revealed while the record is hovered or contains keyboard focus and stays visible on touch screens; at rest it is transparent but keeps its column and its place in the tab order, so the fields never shift. In the stacked layout, it aligns beside the first field at the top of the record.
anatomy.name: Remove action

anatomy.description: Core List's reorder handle, three lines at the end of the record after Remove, in Remove's cell, with an accessible label naming the record and its position and no hover tooltip. Where the primary pointer is coarse, its target grows to at least 44 by 44 px. It is revealed while the record is hovered or contains keyboard focus and stays visible on touch screens; at rest it is transparent but stays in the tab order. In the stacked layout it sits at the top of the record beside Remove. A finger holds it a moment, then drags; a mouse drags at once; activating it (Space or Enter) turns on reorder mode, where Arrow Up and Arrow Down move the record a place and Escape ends the mode.
anatomy.name: Reorder handle

anatomy.description: While a record is in reorder mode, core List's hint anchored to its handle shows the moves and Done as buttons, so taps alone can reorder. Each does what its key does and leaves the focus on the handle.
anatomy.name: Reorder-mode hint

anatomy.description: When no records exist, a centered compact EmptyState names the empty collection and directs users to the Add action.
anatomy.name: Empty state

anatomy.description: Fills the record-fields width, uses the inherited medium control size shared by ListInput fields and actions, and immediately appends a new record created by createItem unless maxItems has been reached. On pointer activation, available vertical scroll containers offset the inserted height from nearest to outermost so the action remains under the pointer; keyboard activation keeps the normal focus behavior, and newly focused field visibility always wins. The live row uses tokenized translate entrance motion when supported, and focus moves to its first field without waiting for the animation.
anatomy.name: Add action

anatomy.description: Explain field-, item-, or list-level errors, warnings, and success states. Field messages use each input's native tooltip status affordance and do not change row height. Item messages align to the record fields without extending under the remove control.
anatomy.name: Validation messages

bestPractices.description: Use stable record keys and consistent columns so focus, validation, and reorder announcements remain attached to the correct record.
Keep validation timing application-owned. Track touched fields by stable item and column keys when errors should appear after blur, while allowing submit or server errors to display immediately.
Place validation at the narrowest useful level: field status for one value, item status for a record-wide problem, and list status for collection-wide requirements.
Forward both status and statusVariant from every column renderer to the rendered Astryx input so field messages use the control's native accessible tooltip pattern.
Let records reorder through the handle: a drag reports one move on release, each key move in reorder mode reports one at once, and focus stays on the handle.

Keep collection motion informational and non-blocking. Added live rows translate into place; removed rows disappear immediately while stable-size survivors close the gap. onChange, focus, and announcements run without waiting, and reduced-motion preferences remain instant.

Keep repeated pointer adding spatially stable by measuring Add before pointer-down blur or validation changes layout, then preserving that viewport position from the nearest vertical scroll container outward. Slight field clipping should not move Add away from the pointer; a meaningfully hidden focused field still takes priority. Keyboard activation follows the normal focus flow.
Use for seven or more records or more than three simple fields per record; use a Table or a dedicated editing flow instead.
Prevent removal solely to enforce a minimum count; allow the action and explain the resulting requirement with list-level validation.

usage.description: ListInput edits a compact, ordered collection of records with consistent fields, built-in add and remove actions, and optional reordering. Standard Astryx controls rendered in its columns inherit the medium control size so inputs align with the Add, remove, reorder, and validation affordances; an explicit field size still takes precedence. Pointer activation measures Add before pointer-down blur or validation can change layout, then keeps it at that viewport position by adjusting available vertical scroll containers from nearest to outermost. The correction is interaction-scoped and rechecked for one animation frame without persistent scroll or resize observation. Added rows enter with tokenized translate motion; after removal, surviving rows animate into their new positions when their geometry stays stable. Motion never delays onChange, focus handoff, or the announcement, while reduced-motion preferences and unsupported browsers use an instant change. Use it for lists with fewer than seven records and up to three simple fields per record, such as guests, travelers, or tag options. Use a Table for larger collections and a card or step-based form when records need many, complex, or inconsistent fields.

doc.description: Video and audio players with themed controls over the browser’s native media element. VideoPlayer and AudioPlayer are ready-made layouts; MediaPlayer, its parts, and useMediaPlayer build custom ones. The native element plays the media, so formats the browser plays need no extra library.

examples.code:
<VideoPlayer
  src="/media/flower.webm"
  label="Bee on a flower"
/>
examples.label: Video player

examples.code:
<VideoPlayer
  src="/media/flower.webm"
  label="Bee on a flower"
  hasAutoPlay
  isLooping
/>
examples.label: Muted autoplay loop

examples.code:
<VideoPlayer
  src="/media/product-tour.mp4"
  poster="/media/product-tour.jpg"
  label="Product tour"
  captions={[
    {src: '/media/product-tour.en.vtt', label: 'English', language: 'en', isDefault: true},

/>

  <HStack gap={1} vAlign="center">

Custom layout

doc.name: MediaPlayer

anatomy.description: A focusable group named by `label`. It scopes keyboard shortcuts, goes fullscreen with its controls, and decides when the controls show.
anatomy.name: Player root

anatomy.description: The native video or audio element with the browser’s controls off. It holds the source, poster, and caption tracks.
anatomy.name: Media element

anatomy.description: In VideoPlayer, a frosted bar 8px from the edges of the video that holds play, the timeline, time, volume, captions, and fullscreen. In a player 480px wide or narrower, volume leaves the bar. In a player 360px wide or narrower, the time leaves it too, and the bar sits 4px from the edges with small buttons, so it covers less of the picture; tooltips and popovers that open from it keep their normal size. It shows on hover, pointer movement, and keyboard focus, and hides after two idle seconds while the video plays. On touch, a tap shows it and the next tap hides it. The volume slider opens beside Mute while Mute is hovered or focused, and always on touch.
anatomy.name: Control bar

anatomy.description: A slider for the playback position. It runs left to right in every direction, because it shows the direction of the media. On the VideoPlayer bar, the part of the track that is neither played nor loaded is a tint of the bar’s accent color, so it shows on the frosted bar with any theme; elsewhere it takes the theme’s track color.
anatomy.name: Timeline

anatomy.description: In VideoPlayer, the large play button before playback, with the control bar hidden, and a replay button after the end, with the control bar shown; a spinner while playback waits for data; and an error message with Try again.
anatomy.name: Status layer

bestPractices.description: Give every player a label that names the media, and give a video caption tracks when it has speech.
Use a poster so the video has a stable first frame and size before it loads.
Keep autoplay for muted, short, or ambient video, and keep a visible pause control for anything that moves longer than five seconds.
Put the control parts in their own MediaPlayer for a custom layout, and keep one play control in the tab order; a second, pointer-only play control takes `tabIndex={-1}` and `aria-hidden`.
Turn on the browser’s own `controls` on the media part, or put two players’ parts in one MediaPlayer.
Rebuild queues, shuffle, or playlists inside the player; compose them in the product around an AudioPlayer.

usage.description: Use VideoPlayer for a video with controls, and AudioPlayer for an episode, recording, or track. For a different layout, put a MediaPlayerElement and the control parts you need inside a MediaPlayer; every part reads the player around it. Keyboard shortcuts work while focus is inside the player: Space or K plays and pauses, M mutes, F toggles fullscreen, C toggles captions, the arrow keys skip 5 seconds and change the volume, J and L skip 10 seconds, 0 to 9 jump to that tenth of the media, and < and > change the speed. Shortcut changes are announced to screen readers. The timeline and volume follow the WAI-ARIA Slider pattern and its Media Seek Slider example; the buttons follow the Button pattern, Captions is a toggle button, and the speed control’s menu variant follows the Menu Button pattern. Streaming formats the browser cannot play, such as DASH, need a streaming library; that library is not part of Lab.

components.description: The navigator. You own the path: pass the entries pushed on the root screen and update them in onPathChange. The stack renders the root screen and one screen per entry, the top one last, keeps covered screens and their scroll positions alive, and makes them inert. The bar shows the top screen's title, its end content and a round Back button with a chevron, named by the screen it returns to. A push moves focus to the new screen's title, unless focus is already in that screen; a pop returns it to the control that pushed the screen. Under a finger the bar paints no background and no hairline, as iOS 26's does. Once a screen's content has moved 10px under the bar, a veil of the body colour fades in at the top of that screen. Each screen keeps its own veil through a push, a pop or a back swipe. With a mouse the bar keeps its surface and hairline.
components.name: NavigationStack

props.description: The root screen, a NavigationScreen. It has no Back button.
props.name: root

props.description: The entries pushed on the root, bottom first. Adding one at the end pushes its screen; removing the last pops it; removing several pops straight back to the new top.
props.name: path

props.description: Called with the new path when a screen pushes or pops (useNavigationStack), Back is pressed, or a back swipe is released past the point of no return.
props.name: onPathChange

props.description: Renders the screen for an entry: a NavigationScreen.
props.name: renderScreen

props.description: A stable key per entry, so a screen keeps its state while others are pushed on it. Defaults to the entry's position.
props.name: getKey

props.description: Whether the back swipe pops: a sideways drag anywhere in the content, under any pointer (a finger, a pen or a mouse drag), and in a web app opened from the home screen also a finger's swipe from the leading screen edge. In a browser tab that edge stays the browser's own back swipe, and on Android the system back owns both screen edges.
props.name: isInteractivePopEnabled

props.description: Accessible name of the navigator region.
props.name: label

components.description: One screen of a NavigationStack: its title, the title Back shows on the screen pushed after it, its end content and its content. Returned by NavigationStack's root and renderScreen; it renders nothing on its own.
components.name: NavigationScreen

props.description: Shown in the bar while the screen is on top, and read first when it arrives.
props.name: title

props.description: What Back reads on the screen pushed on top of this one. Defaults to title.
props.name: backTitle

props.description: How the title shows. 'large' puts it above the content in a large bold type, scrolling with the content; once it has scrolled under the bar, the bar shows the title instead. Use it for a top-level screen, as iOS does.
props.name: titleDisplayMode

props.description: Content at the end of the bar while the screen is on top.
props.name: endContent

props.description: The screen's content. It scrolls on its own and keeps its scroll position while covered.
props.name: children

doc.description: Drill-down navigation for phone layouts: each screen pushes the next on top, and Back, the back swipe from the screen edge or from anywhere in the content returns to the previous one. Pushes, pops and the back swipe move like iOS: the new screen slides in from the trailing edge over the old one, which slides a third as far under a light dimming, and a released swipe finishes or springs back depending on how far and how fast it went. A push never waits for its animation: the new screen is usable as soon as it starts sliding in. With Reduce Motion the screens cross-fade instead. Experimental: lands in lab first.
doc.name: NavigationStack

bestPractices.description: Keep the path in the app's state (or the URL) and give entries stable keys, so screens keep their state as the stack changes.
Push from the control the person activated (a row's onClick): focus returns to it when the screen is popped.
Don't use it for top-level sections that people switch between; those are tabs or a sidebar, which keep each section's own stack.

usage.description: Use NavigationStack for hierarchical drill-down on phones: lists of settings, folders, a list and its detail. Call push from a row with useNavigationStack inside a screen.

doc.description: A row of page indicators under a paging view, as on iOS: one dot per page, the current one highlighted. A tap or a click to either side of the current dot moves one page that way, and sliding a finger or dragging the mouse across the dots scrubs straight to the page under it. Under a finger (any touch device, iOS and Android alike), with more than ten pages the row is a window whose edge dots shrink to show there is more, and a held finger shows a platter behind the dots; with a mouse a long row is cropped to the control. Experimental: lands in lab first.
doc.name: PageControl

props.description: Number of pages.
props.name: totalPages

props.description: Current page number (1-based). Page 1 is the first page.
props.name: page

props.description: Called with the page, 1-based, that a tap, a click, a scrub, an arrow key, Home, End or an assistive technology asks for; a scrub calls it each time the page under the pointer changes, so a quick sweep can skip a page. Update the paging view and page together.
props.name: onChange

props.description: Names the control for assistive technology. Defaults to "Page indicators", localized.
props.name: label

props.description: Render nothing when there is only one page.
props.name: hidesForSinglePage

bestPractices.description: Pair it with a view that pages by swipe: the control is a secondary way to move and the main way to see where you are.
Keep pages few enough to count at a glance; past ten the row stays a fixed width, shows a window of them and scrolls as the page changes.
Don't use it for long lists of results (use Pagination) or for choosing between views (use SegmentedControl or TabList).

usage.description: Use PageControl below a paging view, such as a Carousel with `hasSnap` or onboarding screens, to show how many pages there are and which one is showing. Keep its page in step with the view in both directions.

props.description: The view object that owns the layout and the date range each page covers. Build one with createScheduleMonthlyView, createScheduleWeeklyView, createScheduleDayView, or createScheduleListView; each factory takes its own options (weekStartsOn, minHour/maxHour/hourHeight, days). The week, day, and month factories also take renderPopover(event): return the content for an event and the view renders that event as a button that opens a popover it manages — one popover for the view, named by the event title, with the system's standard surface, padding, Escape and light dismiss, and focus return; return null to leave an event read-only. In the month view that popover also shows a busy day's list, and a row in the list opens its event in place. The list view has no interaction option.
props.name: view

props.description: Either a static array, filtered to the events overlapping the rendered range and sorted by start, or a loader called with that range's start and end epoch milliseconds. A loader suspends while pending; the header shows a spinner and the view renders empty. Results are cached per loader identity and range, so keep the loader reference stable (useCallback) or every re-render refetches. When your page already holds the events, pass them as an array; Schedule picks out each range's events without a loader.
props.name: events

props.description: Category definitions matched to each event by label === event.category. The match supplies the event's color and the category name in its accessible label. An event whose category names no entry keeps that name but falls back to blue; an event with no category is announced as "Event" in blue. A category can stand for any grouping you color by — an event kind, a calendar, or a team; to color events by calendar, give each calendar its own entry.
props.name: categories

props.description: Unix epoch milliseconds anywhere inside the range to render; the view expands it to a full month, week, day, or list window. Fully controlled; Schedule never changes it, so pair it with onChangeDate.
props.name: date

props.description: Unix epoch milliseconds marking the day treated as "today": in the month, week, and day views that cell gets aria-current="date" and the highlighted styling. The list view ignores it. When omitted it is captured once at mount and never advances afterwards.
props.name: focusDate

props.description: Called with the epoch milliseconds to render next when a pagination plugin pages backward or forward, or when Today is pressed. Paging preserves the time of day; Today passes the current time.
props.name: onChangeDate

props.description: IANA timezone ID (e.g. "America/Los_Angeles") used for every date calculation and every formatted label, so the same events regroup across days when it changes.
props.name: timezoneID

props.description: Header plugins, applied in order; each may wrap or replace the start, center, and end header content. Supplying an array replaces the default pagination controls; compose useSchedulePaginationPlugin and useScheduleViewSelectorPlugin to keep both.
props.name: plugins

props.description: Heading level for sub-headings inside the schedule (the weekday and day column headers in the grid views, and the day headings in the list view), so the schedule nests correctly under the surrounding page outline. The header range title is always a level-2 heading.
props.name: headingLevel

anatomy.description: Leading header region filled by plugins. The default plugin set renders a previous / Today / next button group here.
anatomy.name: Header start slot

anatomy.description: A level-2 heading naming the range on screen, e.g. "May 2026". The same text is the accessible name of the schedule region.
anatomy.name: Header title

anatomy.description: Sits beside the title while an async events loader is still pending, labelled "Loading events".
anatomy.name: Loading spinner

anatomy.description: Trailing header region, empty by default. The view selector plugin renders its menu here.
anatomy.name: Header end slot

anatomy.description: Whatever the view renders: a month grid, a day/week time grid with an hour gutter and an all-day row, or a list grouped under day headings. Grid views expose ARIA grid, columnheader, and gridcell roles and are marked aria-readonly. The day/week time grid scrolls inside one keyboard-reachable region named after the range; its day header, all-day row, and hour gutter stay pinned while the columns scroll. The all-day row also holds timed events that last 24 hours or more, as one span across their days.
anatomy.name: View body

anatomy.description: One pill (grid views) or row with a color dot (list view) per event, tinted by its category and dimmed once it is in the past. In the day and week grids, events that happen at the same time share the column side by side, and when the view is built with renderPopover each event with content is a button that opens the view's popover. In the month grid a week row shows at most three levels of chips; a busy day shows two and a "+N more" button that opens a popover listing every event of that day. A month chip leads with the title; the start time of a timed event follows it only when both fit. When the month view is built with renderPopover, each chip with content is a button that opens the same popover as its day's "+N more", and each later day a chip covers names its event for screen readers.
anatomy.name: Event

anatomy.description: A line across the day or week time grid at the current time, on the current day only. It ticks once a minute and is absent during server rendering. When the rendered range includes today, the grid opens scrolled to one hour before this line (clamped to the grid) once per range, and then leaves the scroll position alone until the person pages to another range or switches views.
anatomy.name: Current time line

bestPractices.description: Hold the rendered date in state and wire onChangeDate to it. Schedule never advances the date itself, so without that handler the built-in previous/Today/next controls render but nothing moves.
Match the view to the density of the data: a month grid for at-a-glance load, a day or week time grid when start and end times matter, a list when the schedule is sparse.

Wrap Schedule in InternationalizationProvider to choose the language, numbering, and field order used by its date and time labels; the provider calendar, such as calendar="persian", writes those labels in another calendar. Schedule date values, its grids, and its date navigation stay Gregorian in every calendar and locale.
Give each event a category string that matches a categories entry so its color is meaningful and screen readers announce the category name. An unmatched name still renders, but always in blue.
Reach for Schedule when the user has to pick a date. It has no selection model; use DateInput, DateRangeInput, or Calendar instead.
Rely on event color alone to carry meaning. Only ten colors exist, so they repeat on larger category sets; the accessible label already announces title, category, and time.

When your page already pages the range with its own controls, keep date in your state and pass plugins={[]}: Schedule then renders the range title with no controls of its own, and your controls call the same setter as onChangeDate.
Pass a custom plugins array without useSchedulePaginationPlugin when you still want Schedule's previous, Today, and next controls; a custom array replaces the default set rather than extending it.

usage.description: Schedule is a calendar surface that renders events as a month grid, a day or week time grid, or a list grouped by day: the layout comes from a view object you pass in. It handles timezone-aware date math, paging between ranges, and async event loading, and exposes header slots that plugins fill with navigation controls. Use it to display an existing schedule; build the week, day, or month view with renderPopover to let people open an event's details in a popover the view manages. It has no event selection, creation, or editing affordances.

doc.description: A set of selectable cards with the semantics of its selection. One choice (the default) is a radio group: the cards are native radios sharing one name, so the set is one tab stop, the arrow keys move and select, and screen readers speak the position ("2 of 3"). Several choices are a named group of checkboxes. Each SelectableCardGroupItem is a SelectableCard whose input, name and selection come from the group.
doc.name: SelectableCardGroup

props.description: The group's visible label and accessible name.
props.name: label

props.description: `single`: a radio group with one value. `multiple`: a group of checkboxes with any number of values.
props.name: type

props.description: The chosen value (`single`, `null` while none is chosen) or values (`multiple`).
props.name: value

props.description: Called with the chosen value (`single`) or the new list of values (`multiple`).
props.name: onChange

props.description: Hides the label visually; it still names the group.
props.name: isLabelHidden

props.description: Helper text under the label, linked to the group.
props.name: description

props.description: The name the group's value is submitted under. The radios group by a generated name. Defaults to a generated one.
props.name: htmlName

props.description: Disables every card; they stay focusable and announce disabled.
props.name: isDisabled

props.description: `horizontal` wraps the cards in rows; `vertical` stacks them.
props.name: orientation

props.description: SelectableCardGroupItem cards. Each takes a `value` and the SelectableCard props other than isSelected and onChange.
props.name: children

props.description: StyleX styles for the Field box around the label, description and cards (margins, positioning, sizing). The group composes Field, so it takes no root xstyle, className or style.
props.name: containerXstyle

props.description: Class name for the Field box. Same targeting as containerXstyle.
props.name: containerClassName

props.description: Inline styles for the Field box. Same targeting as containerXstyle.
props.name: containerStyle

bestPractices.description: Give every card a `label` that names its option; it is the radio or checkbox name screen readers speak.
Start a single choice with a value when the product has a sensible default, so the tab stop lands on it.
Put buttons or links inside the cards; the whole card is the radio or checkbox target.
Use it for navigation or actions; use ClickableCard for those.

usage.description: Use it for a choice among a few rich options shown as cards: a plan, an appearance, a layout. One choice gives users the radio-group keyboard and the position they expect; use `multiple` when several cards can be on.

dense.description: KPI/metric display: label, large tabular-nums value, sentiment-aware delta, and trend media slot.

propDescriptions.delta: Direction glyph + colored change text; sentiment overrides direction colors.
propDescriptions.description: Muted supporting line under the value.
propDescriptions.label: Metric name above the value.
propDescriptions.media: Trend slot below the text (sparkline/mini chart).
propDescriptions.xstyle: StyleX layout styles; must be stylex.create() value.

bestPractices.description: Pass pre-formatted strings for value and delta ("1.2M", "+12.4%"); Stat does not format numbers.
Set `sentiment` explicitly for inverted metrics where down is good, like error rate or latency.
Wrap Stat in a Card and lay out KPI rows with Grid columns={{minWidth: 240, max: 4}}.
Put a full-size chart in the media slot; it is meant for compact sparklines or trend glyphs.
Rely on delta color alone to convey meaning; the direction glyph and screen-reader text carry it too.

usage.description: A KPI/metric display for dashboards and summary rows: metric name, large tabular-nums value, an optional sentiment-aware delta, a supporting description, and a media slot for a sparkline or mini chart. Compose several in a Grid for a KPI row.

props.description: Metric name shown above the value, e.g. "Total requests".
props.name: label

props.description: Headline metric rendered large with tabular numerals. Pass a pre-formatted string like "1.2M".
props.name: value

props.name: delta

props.description: Muted supporting line under the value, e.g. "vs. previous 30 days".
props.name: description

props.description: Trend slot rendered below the text content, e.g. a sparkline or mini chart. Stat does not render a chart itself.
props.name: media

props.description: Size variant controlling the value's font size.
props.name: size

props.description: StyleX styles for layout customization (margins, positioning, sizing). Must be a stylex.create() value, not an inline style object like style={{}}.

bestPractices.description: Pass pre-formatted strings for value and delta ("1.2M", "+12.4%"); Stat does not format numbers.
Set `sentiment` explicitly for inverted metrics where down is good, like error rate or latency.
Wrap Stat in a Card and lay out KPI rows with Grid columns={{minWidth: 240, max: 4}}.
Put a full-size chart in the media slot; it is meant for compact sparklines or trend glyphs.
Rely on delta color alone to convey meaning; the direction glyph and screen-reader text carry it too.

usage.description: A KPI/metric display for dashboards and summary rows: metric name, large tabular-nums value, an optional sentiment-aware delta, a supporting description, and a media slot for a sparkline or mini chart. Compose several in a Grid for a KPI row.

components.description: The bar. It sits fixed at the bottom of the viewport, over the page, so leave 83 px of room at the bottom of the scrolling content, and declare it on LayerProvider (inset={{blockEnd: 83}}) so menus, popovers and toasts clear it. You own the selection: pass the selected tab's value and update it in onChange.
components.name: TabBar

props.description: The selected tab's value.
props.name: value

props.description: Called with a tab's value when a different tab is chosen: a finger lifted over it (after a tap or a drag across the bar), a click, or Enter or Space on a focused tab.
props.name: onChange

props.description: Called with the selected tab's value when it is chosen again, for example to return the tab's navigation stack to its root, as iOS does. On every reselect TabBar also scrolls the tab's panel (panelId) to its top.
props.name: onReselect

props.description: Names the tab bar for assistive technology. Without it, or aria-label or aria-labelledby (which win over it and reach the tab list), the tab list is named "Tabs" in the reader's language.
props.name: label

props.description: The tabs: TabBarItem elements, in order, as direct children. With more than five, the bar shows the first four and a More tab that holds the rest.
props.name: children

props.description: The More tab's value, with more than five tabs. Choosing More calls onChange with it (and onReselect while More holds a tab, to return to its list); More reads as selected while value is moreValue or any tab past the fourth. Render TabBarMoreList while value is moreValue, and a section chosen there inside More's own navigation stack.
props.name: moreValue

components.description: One tab: its value, label, icon and badge. TabBar reads its props and draws it; it renders nothing on its own.
components.name: TabBarItem

props.description: Identifies the tab in value, onChange and onReselect.
props.name: value

props.description: The tab's name, shown under its icon. Keep it to one short word.
props.name: label

props.description: The tab's icon, an Icon at size lg. It is drawn in the current text colour, and in the accent colour while selected.
props.name: icon

props.description: The icon while the tab is selected, typically its filled variant. Defaults to icon.
props.name: selectedIcon

props.description: A badge over the icon's top-trailing corner: a count or a short string such as "!". It appears, changes and disappears without animating. Omit it or pass an empty string for none.
props.name: badge

props.description: What assistive technology reads for the badge after the tab's label, such as "3 unread". Defaults to the badge itself.
props.name: badgeLabel

props.description: Id of the panel this tab controls, wired up as aria-controls. Put the same id on the section's panel element. Choosing the selected tab again scrolls that panel to its top: the panel itself when it scrolls, or else the first scroll area inside it.
props.name: panelId

props.description: Disables the tab, as on Core's Tab: it stays focusable but dimmed and is never chosen. A tap, a click or a key on it, or a lift over it, selects nothing, and the arrow keys skip it. A finger that lands on it lifts no lens until it drags or reaches an enabled tab, which the lift then chooses. This differs from iOS on purpose. iOS ignores a touch that starts on a disabled tab, but TabBar follows the action-group rule: the tab you lift on acts.
props.name: aria-disabled

doc.description: The bottom tab bar of a phone app, as on iOS 26: the app's top-level sections as a floating capsule above the bottom edge, with a selection lens that slides to the chosen tab. Each tab has an icon, a label and an optional badge. Under a finger, on iOS and Android alike, it behaves like iOS 26's: the lens lifts into glass as a finger lands, follows a finger dragged across the tabs and settles on the tab nearest where it lifts, while the bar flexes; under a mouse, a press is a plain button press: a click chooses a tab and the lens follows the theme's motion. With no tab selected, a held finger highlights the tab under it. Choosing the selected tab again scrolls its panel to the top and is reported separately, so a screen can also return to its root as iOS does. With more than five tabs the bar shows the first four and a More tab, and TabBarMoreList lists the rest. Experimental: lands in lab first.
doc.name: TabBar

bestPractices.description: Keep every tab visible and the set stable; give each a short label and an outline icon with a filled selectedIcon.
Keep to five tabs where you can; with more, put the sections people use most first, since the rest move into More.
Use a badge for something that needs attention in that section, such as unread items, and say what it counts in badgeLabel.

Give each tab a panelId naming its section's panel, so assistive technology can associate the two. Put the section's content in a ScrollableArea inside that panel, so choosing the tab again scrolls it to the top.
Disable a tab only while its section cannot open, and keep it in place, so the other tabs do not move.
Don't use it for actions, for filters within one screen (use SegmentedControl) or for tabs inside a page (use TabList).

usage.description: Use TabBar to switch between an app's three to five top-level sections on a phone, each keeping its own state and navigation stack. Keep each section's navigation stack in the app and return it to its root in onReselect.

doc.description: The More tab's screen, as on iOS: one row per tab past the fourth, with its icon, its label and a disclosure chevron. Give it the same TabBarItem children as TabBar, and render it while TabBar's value is its moreValue. A disabled tab's row is disabled too. Rearranging the tabs (iOS's Edit) is not available yet. Experimental: lands in lab first.
doc.name: TabBarMoreList

props.description: The same TabBarItem elements given to TabBar.
props.name: children

props.description: Called with a row's value when it is chosen: show that section inside More, which stays selected in the bar.
props.name: onChange

props.description: The selected tab's value: its row reads as selected.
props.name: value

bestPractices.description: Give it the same tabs, in the same order, as the TabBar it belongs to.
Don't use it as a general menu or list; use List for those.

usage.description: Render TabBarMoreList as the More tab's screen while TabBar's value is its moreValue, with the same TabBarItem children. Show a section chosen there inside More's own navigation stack.

components.description: Controller for a guided tour. Coordinates the active step among its TourStep children, exposes advance / retreat / complete / dismiss, and optionally dims the page around the active step (spotlight cutout). Controlled via isActive: the consumer owns "has this user seen the tour?".
components.name: Tour

props.description: Whether the tour is running. When false nothing renders and the tour resets to the first step, so it restarts cleanly next time it becomes active.
props.name: isActive

props.description: The tour steps: TourStep elements. Step order follows their order here; only the active step renders its callout.
props.name: children

props.description: Called on every exit, with the reason ('backdrop' | 'escape' | 'close' | 'skip' | 'complete'). The consumer flips isActive to false in response, and can branch on the source to distinguish a successful finish from an early exit.
props.name: onDismiss

props.description: Dim the page around the active step as a spotlight cutout: the target stays lit while everything else darkens. While the page is dimmed, a press anywhere outside the callout, the target included, ends the tour with "backdrop". Use for modal-style steps that demand focus; leave off for a lightweight coachmark that only rings the target, or for a step whose target the user should press.
props.name: hasBackdrop

props.description: Show the step count ("2 of 5") in each step.
props.name: isStepCountShown

components.description: A single spotlight step. Highlights a target element with a ring drawn as a separate overlay (the target is never restyled) and renders a non-modal callout anchored to it, with a heading, body, optional step progress, and back / next / close controls. The callout is a region named by its heading. Focus moves to it when the step starts, and Tab can leave it for the page, so a step can introduce a control the user then operates. Without a backdrop, pressing the target or the page leaves the tour running; Escape ends it. Registers with the parent Tour on mount and renders its callout only while active.
components.name: TourStep

props.description: Ref to the element this step points at: any element, such as a button, a card, a table cell or a chart region. The callout sits beside it. The target keeps its own behavior: without a backdrop, pressing it does not end the tour, and keyboard focus can reach it while the step shows. Under the backdrop of the Tour, a press on the target ends the tour with "backdrop".
props.name: targetRef

props.description: Step heading.
props.name: heading

props.description: Step body content.
props.name: children

props.description: Which side of the target the callout sits on.
props.name: placement

props.description: How the callout aligns along the placement side (e.g. with placement="below": start left-aligns under the target, center centers, end right-aligns).
props.name: alignment

doc.description: A guided product tour (NUX / onboarding). Tour is a controller that steps a user through a sequence of spotlight callouts anchored to elements on the page. It renders no chrome itself; it owns the active-step state and shares it with declaratively-nested TourStep children (step order follows the children). Experimental: lands in lab first (meta/astryx#4239).
doc.name: Tour

bestPractices.description: Keep tours short: a few high-value steps. Long tours get skipped.
Persist completion yourself (from onDismiss) so a user does not see the same tour on every visit.
Point each step at a stable, visible element; ensure the target is on-screen before its step becomes active.
Gate essential, must-see information behind a tour step; users can dismiss it; put critical info inline.
Use a tour as a substitute for clear UI; fix confusing interfaces rather than narrating them.

usage.description: Use a Tour to introduce a feature or onboard a user through a few key parts of the UI. Compose it from TourStep children, each pointing at an element via targetRef; the Tour advances through them with Next/Back and ends on Done. It is controlled: keep isActive in your own state and persist "has seen this tour" yourself (the component only reports dismissal via onDismiss). Built on the existing layer anchoring and overlay tokens rather than a bespoke positioning engine.

Use direct TransferList plus ComplexSelector only for custom saved views, presets, headers, or actions; reset draft from applied value on open.

Use commitBehavior for presentation/container choice; both values use the selector popover.
Use for a few simple choices; prefer CheckboxInput.

props.description: Makes the selected options reorderable: pass the object createReorderable makes. Each selected row ends with a reorder handle: on a touch screen hold the handle for a moment, then drag; a mouse drags at once; a tap, a click, Space or Enter on a handle turns on reorder mode for its row, in which each arrow key (or each move in the hint below the handle) moves it a place, and Escape, Done or another activation ends the mode, keeping the moves. The object's isReorderable(value) says which values move: one it rejects has no handle, and at either end of the selected list it also keeps the others from moving past it. In immediate behavior each move goes to the object's onReorder({key, to}); in staged behavior the selector moves its draft instead, so Cancel drops the move with the draft and Apply commits it through onChange. Reordering pauses while a search filters the panel. Without it, the selected options keep their order.

anatomy.name: Field label and description

anatomy.name: Selector trigger

anatomy.description: Filters the selected and available lists without changing their values and uses a uniform 12px inset.
anatomy.name: Search

anatomy.description: Places two unframed semantic lists beside one divider. Narrow containers stack the sections, use the body background behind each column header, expand both sections to their rows, and delegate overflow to one scrollable containing surface.
anatomy.name: Selected and available sections
